source.title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics

accepted.question_text: How can gravity and quantum physics be made to coexist within a single logically consistent theory, given that quantum physics and general relativity already overlap each other's domains but do not fit together, and how can such a theory be tested when the direct experiments needed are beyond present technology?

evidence.quote: The biggest unsolved problem in fundamental physics is how gravity and the quantum will be made to coexist within the same theory.
The problem is that quantum physics and general relativity already overlap each other’s domains, but do not fit together.
The biggest challenge with quantum gravity, from a scientific point of view, is that we cannot do the experiments required.

accepted.question_text: Why do the elementary particles have the particular masses they have, when the standard model contains many free parameters whose values cannot be calculated or predicted theoretically, and why do there exist heavier second- and third-generation copies of the first-generation matter particles that appear identical except for mass even though ordinary matter consists only of first-generation particles?

evidence.quote: These parameters cannot be calculated or predicted theoretically.
From a theoretical point of view, then, the particle masses are a total mystery - they might as well have been random numbers drawn from a hat.

The first generation - which contains the electron, the electron-neutrino, the up-quark and the down-quark are followed by two additional copies which appear identical in everything except their masses. Ourselves and everything we know of, both on earth and in the cosmos, consist only of particles from the first generation. What are the heavier ones for?

accepted.question_text: How and why does a quantum measurement make a particle's wave function collapse to a single definite outcome, and how does the definite macroscopic world we observe arise from a microscopic quantum description in which many states coexist in superposition and linear evolution alone would allow those coexisting states to persist forever?

evidence.quote: But how and why does a measurement on a particle make its wave function collapse, which in turn produces the concrete reality we perceive?
Why then do we not see ghostly superpositions of objects even at our level? This problem is still unsolved.

Without additional assumptions beyond quantum physics, nothing can ever happen! This is because the wave function mathematically is described by so-called linear equations, where states that have ever coexisted will do so forever.

accepted.question_text: Do general solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluids exist, and if they do, are they free of singularities and sufficient to describe turbulent fluid motion; more broadly, is turbulence ultimately understandable within human mathematical and physical methods or not?

evidence.quote: In fact, it is not known whether a general solution to the Navier-Stokes equations (for incompressible fluids) even exists, and, if there is a solution, whether it fully describes the fluid or contains unknowable points - singularities.
The kind of chaos inherent in turbulence - in both time and space - is still a mystery [4].
Does turbulence exceed the human physical understanding and mathematical ability, or would it become intelligible if only we tackled it with the right methods?

accepted.question_text: What is dark energy, if the apparent accelerated expansion of the universe is interpreted as requiring a previously unknown form of cosmic energy, and does dark energy in fact exist as a real physical component of the universe at all?

evidence.quote: The surprise was therefore total when the observational data instead seemed to indicate that the universe is accelerating, i.e. increases its rate of expansion - as if the cosmos recently moved its foot from the brake pedal to the accelerator.
The best fit to the cosmological standard model ... showed that about 70% of the energy of the universe seemed to be of a completely unknown form, which has been named Dark Energy.
The mystery is that no one still knows what dark energy is (or if it even exists).

accepted.question_text: What is the dark matter whose existence has been inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation, and cosmic structure formation, if it exists at all, and can it be directly detected or identified among candidate forms such as weakly interacting massive particles or massive compact halo objects?

evidence.quote: Other observations indicate that about 90 percent of the matter itself in the universe is made up of an exotic, unknown variety that neither absorbs nor emits light.
Instead, the existence of dark matter is still hypothetical [8] and its large abundance derived from its gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation and structure formation in the universe.

This strange invisible matter is thought to not only permeate the outskirts of galaxies, but the entire universe and may, possibly, consist of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) or massive compact halo objects (MACHOs). There are today several experiments around the world in search of them.

accepted.question_text: Can the behavior of even mildly complex systems be derived in detail from the four known fundamental forces alone, or must physics be supplemented by additional principles at larger scales; in particular, how should one explain self-organization, the origin of life, what life is, and how consciousness can arise from matter if reduction to fundamental laws is not by itself enough?

evidence.quote: Although the four known fundamental forces of nature (gravity, electromagnetism, strong nuclear and weak nuclear) are all relatively simple, it is almost always impossible to directly from them in detail predict the behavior of even mildly complex systems.

The logical possibility also exist that the world is not reductionist (or rather, constructionist), that is, that a handful of fundamental laws are not sufficient to build up (reconstruct) all the complexity that we see around us, but rather that these may have to be supplemented by new (unknown) principles on different scales.

Many believe that this field of research will be essential for understanding and explaining phenomena such as the origin of life (and what life really is) and how consciousness seemingly miraculously can arise from mindless atoms in the brain.

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism produced the small excess of matter over antimatter in the early universe, given the expectation that the Big Bang should have produced matter and antimatter symmetrically and given that the known CP-violation is far too weak to explain the matter-dominated universe observed today?

evidence.quote: The question of why there is so much more matter than its oppositely charged mirror image, antimatter, is actually the crucial question of why anything exists at all [10].
Thus, the Big Bang should have produced equal parts matter and antimatter.
The problem is that the known CP-violation is far too weak and insignificant to explain why we today have only matter.

accepted.question_text: How does macroscopic friction arise in a world made entirely of atoms when the microscopic quantum description itself contains no friction, and why do frictional macroscopic processes display an obvious preferred direction of time even though microscopic frictionless interactions can be run equally well forward or backward?

evidence.quote: It may seem strange and surprising that in physics we still do not understand how something so 'obvious' as friction arises. But at the microscopic atomic level there is no friction, this can be easily seen by ogling the basic formula of quantum physics - the Schrödinger equation. Everything, however, consists of atoms, so how can friction then appear on our level?
On a microscopic frictionless level, one can freely reverse the temporal direction and still get a perfectly possible behavior.
But if we instead see a hockey puck that glides along the ice and stops (due to friction), we can immediately sense if the movie runs forwards or backwards.

accepted.question_text: What explains the arrow of time, namely the fact that time appears to move forward for macroscopic systems, and more specifically why was the entropy of the universe so low in the past so that the universe began in such an ordered state; relatedly, is time as represented in current physical theories perhaps not fundamental but an illusion?

evidence.quote: It is sometimes argued that time moves forward due to the fact that a property of the universe called entropy, defined as the degree of disorder, never decreases for a macroscopic system.
But the underlying and unresolved question then becomes: why was the entropy so low in the past?
Maybe even time, as we so far have described it in our theories, is really just an illusion [13]?
